analysis.one_liner: Permanently bans offshore oil and gas drilling along the Atlantic Coast and the Straits of Florida.
analysis.headline: The bill drew 28 cosponsors from both parties and got a subcommittee hearing, but never received a committee or floor vote and died when the 117th Congress ended in January 2023.
analysis.plain_summary: The COAST Anti-Drilling Act would have permanently barred the Interior Department from leasing or authorizing oil and gas drilling in four federal offshore zones: the North Atlantic, Mid-Atlantic, South Atlantic, and the Straits of Florida. Its aim was to protect Atlantic beaches, coastal tourism, and fishing from oil spills and drilling infrastructure. It never left the House Natural Resources Committee.
analysis.who_benefits: Coastal communities along the Atlantic seaboard and Florida, plus the tourism, hospitality, and fishing businesses that depend on clean beaches and healthy fisheries, would gain protection from oil spills and offshore drilling activity. Beachgoers and coastal residents would also avoid the industrialization of the Atlantic coastline.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Atlantic coastal communities, tourism, and fishing businesses

how_it_helps.text: Permanently prohibits the Interior Department from issuing any lease or authorization for exploration, development, or production of oil, gas, or minerals in the North Atlantic, Mid-Atlantic, South Atlantic, and Straits of Florida planning areas, amending the Outer Continental Shelf Lands Act so the ban is written into law rather than left to each administration's discretion.
Shields Atlantic beaches and coastal waters from the risk of oil spills and drilling infrastructure, protecting the tourism economies the bill's own name — Clean Ocean And Safe Tourism — points to.
Removes the threat of new offshore drilling for fishing interests, since a major spill or routine drilling activity can damage marine and coastal fisheries.

analysis.who_pays: Oil and gas companies lose potential access to the Atlantic outer continental shelf, and the federal government forgoes whatever lease bonuses and royalties those sales might have brought in. Consumers would be only marginally affected, and the bill leaves the Gulf of Mexico — where most U.S. offshore drilling already happens — untouched.
analysis.who_pays_short: Oil and gas companies; forgone lease revenue

drawbacks.text: A permanent statutory ban takes the decision away from case-by-case leasing reviews and future administrations, which critics say is too rigid even if Atlantic drilling is unwise today; it would also reduce potential domestic production and federal lease revenue at a time of energy-price sensitivity.

The bill is geographic, not an energy policy: it leaves the Gulf of Mexico open to drilling, so offshore production and spill risk would simply continue in the Gulf rather than being reduced nationwide.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For Atlantic coastal states the benefit is concrete — a legal guarantee their beaches and fisheries cannot be opened to drilling — while the cost falls mostly on an industry that was not currently producing in those waters anyway. The main honest criticism is that a permanent ban is a blunt instrument and that the bill does nothing about drilling in the Gulf of Mexico, where most U.S. offshore production actually occurs.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Natural Resources Committee and its Energy and Mineral Resources Subcommittee, which held one hearing three days after introduction, and then nothing more happened before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Frank Pallone introduced the bill on May 11, 2021, with 22 original cosponsors, and it was referred to the House Committee on Natural Resources the same day.
The next day it was referred to the Subcommittee on Energy and Mineral Resources, and the subcommittee held a hearing on May 13, 2021.
After that hearing the bill saw no further action — no subcommittee vote, no full committee markup, no floor vote — and support grew to 28 cosponsors, 25 Democrats and 3 Republicans.
The bill died quietly when the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023, as any bill that has not passed both chambers does.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Oil and gas companies are better off, since nothing now stands in the way of a future administration proposing Atlantic leases; the Atlantic's protection remained only the temporary executive withdrawal in place at the time, not the permanent legal ban this bill would have created.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Oil and gas companies, which keep potential Atlantic access

for.name: Rep. Frank Pallone
for.what_they_did: Introduced the COAST Anti-Drilling Act to permanently ban Atlantic and Straits of Florida offshore drilling.

for.name: Rep. Raúl Grijalva
for.what_they_did: Signed on as an original cosponsor of the bill in the committee with jurisdiction over it.

for.name: Reps. John Rutherford (FL), Jeff Van Drew (NJ), and Chris Smith (NJ)
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, making it one of the few energy bills with Republican coastal-state support.

against.name: House Democratic leadership
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the House floor for a vote, even with 28 cosponsors and a subcommittee hearing on record.

against.name: Oil and gas industry trade groups
against.what_they_did: Consistently opposed permanent offshore drilling bans that would close the Atlantic outer continental shelf to leasing.

sides.party_line_note: The bill never got a roll-call vote, but its support in the record was 28 cosponsors, 25 Democrats and 3 Republicans — nearly all Democrats, with a handful of coastal-district Republicans joining.

industries.note: The bill would permanently close the North Atlantic, Mid-Atlantic, South Atlantic, and Straits of Florida planning areas to leasing, ending any prospect of Atlantic production; the industry keeps the Gulf of Mexico, which the bill does not touch. Its interest in keeping those waters open runs against the coastal tourism and fishing economies the ban protects.

Beach towns from New Jersey to Florida depend on clean coastlines; a permanent drilling ban protects the beaches and ocean views their visitors pay for. An oil spill anywhere near the coast hits exactly these businesses.
Fishing fleets and seafood businesses face direct losses from spills and seismic surveying; the bill removes drilling from the waters they work.
